podcast.title: Band Name Origin
podcast.body: The Bay City Rollers randomly chose their name from a town in Michigan, believing an American name sounded "cool." Previously, they had been known as The Saxons. "They took their name from a town in Michigan at random because an American name sounded cool they had been known as the Saxons."

podcast.title: Briefly Labeled "Punk" (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: In the mid-1970s, as the term "punk rock" was being used carelessly, even the Bay City Rollers were, at one point, called "punks." "Even the Bay City Rollers were called punks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Discrepancy Between Image and Reality
podcast.body: The band's wholesome image was a stark contrast to their behind-the-scenes behavior, which included drug use and sex. While such behavior might be expected of rock bands like Led Zeppelin or The Who, it was not accepted for a famous boy band, where image was paramount. Les McKeown commented on the "shattered illusion" of his "milk drinking clean living virgin" persona. "Les McHughan said in the 70s I was the milk drinking clean living virgin that the Bay City Rollers manager made me when that illusion was shattered. I was the drug crazed hell raising fallen idle that the press made me..."

podcast.title: Fan Defense After Poor Performance
podcast.body: Following a poorly reviewed concert in Ottawa in August 1976, where the band mixed up songs, young fans deluged the *Ottawa Citizen* with letters to the editor, defending the band by attributing their mistakes to nervousness and excitement. "The review of the show was not kind this unleashed a torrent of letters to the editor of the Ottawa citizen from their young fans. One wrote that she is sure that the boys were just a little bit nervous and excited."

podcast.title: Fan Loyalty Amidst Scandals
podcast.body: Despite revelations that the band members smoked, did not drink milk, and one even hit an old woman with his car, fans' loyalty to the Bay City Rollers remained undiminished. "And even when learning that the Bay City Rollers they did not really drink milk and they did in fact smoke and one of them hit an old woman with his car. None of that really seemed to dampen the fans loyalty to the band."

podcast.title: Managerial Image Control and Abuse
podcast.body: Manager Tam Paton meticulously crafted the band's image as "clean living Scottish boys" in calf-length pants and tartan scarves to appeal to young teenage girls. He maintained strict control over this image, even firing band members as he saw fit. Paton also reportedly fed the boys speed, stole their money, and faced disturbing allegations of attempted rape and later went to prison for molesting other underage boys. "Their manager tampatin invented stories about them being these clean living Scottish boys and calf like pants and tartan scarves to make them appealing to the 13 year old to bottle the teen idle magazines and skated to their songs at the roller ring. He created their image and he kept a very tight control of it firing members of the band whenever it suited him."

podcast.title: Mid-70s Boy Band Equivalent
podcast.body: The Bay City Rollers are described as the "mid-70s equivalent of a modern boy band like One Direction," highlighting their pop appeal and mass fan base. "These are the Basidy Rollers, the mid-70s equivalent of a modern boy band like One Direction."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Simplistic Pop Appeal (Early 1970s)
podcast.body: Represented the "simplistic pop" that entranced the generation following the hippies, much to the dismay of older music fans. "The generation following them seemed to be totally entranced by simplistic pop made by David Cassidy and Bobby Sherman and the Bay City Rollers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Unprecedented Fan Hysteria
podcast.body: In 1977, at the height of their popularity, rock journalist Lisa Robinson noted that the level of hysteria generated by the Bay City Rollers was surprising and unprecedented, surpassing even that of The Osmonds or David Cassidy, despite her belief that Americans were too sophisticated for such a "boy band." "The level of hysteria generated by them was surprising to her as she thought that Americans were too sophisticated as she put it to be taken in by a boy band like that."
